title: AI and the future of work
text:
Everyone is anxious about AI and how it will displace their job, upend their life.  There are many thoughts about this from a dystopian world to a more gradual transition over decades. The truth is probably somewhere in between, and it really depends on where you are in your personal career journey. However, society (from gov't to corporate America) needs to make contingency plans. Here is one very modest proposal.

https://www.nytimes.com/2025/12/27/opinion/artificial-intelligence-jobs-worker-training.html?smid=url-share

title: Perspectives on health and medicine
text:
Our healthcare system is not serving the American public as it could. The politics are entrenched and perverse. This is a solvable crisis brewing over decades and our "values" do not permit getting to universal coverage for all people. We practice "welfare chauvinism", a new term for me as noted in this opinion piece.  The efforts at any incremental expansion of coverage have been blocked. Who can with a straight face say they do not wish some form of universal care?  
The upcoming loss of coverage for millions and the politics will preoccupy us in 2026 till the mid-terms.

title: Breakneck: China's engineering ambitions
text:
Just read this fascinating book (quick read) that offers an interesting framework on the China - US dichotomy.

Wang claims that because China’s leadership and technocratic elite are engineers, decisions tilt toward construction and rapid execution. In contrast, U.S. policymakers trained in law elevate deliberation, compliance, and procedural checks, which slows action. China’s massive infrastructure and manufacturing capabilities aren’t incidental — they are instruments of national power. Wang shows how building capacity (e.g., EVs, semiconductor supply chains, nationwide rail) translates into geopolitical leverage. The same engineering mindset that builds megacities also tries to engineer people — resulting in harsh social policies, intense surveillance, and political repression. Wang doesn’t romanticize China; he highlights these trade-offs.  

Portrayal of the U.S. as merely “lawyerly” lacks depth and nuance compared to the richly detailed depiction of China’s engineering state. The American side risks caricature. The emphasis on legal caution can be reframed: protecting individual rights, environmental standards, and democratic accountability isn’t simply obstruction — it’s a foundation for sustainable and equitable societies that the “engineer state” approach too often sacrifices.

This book offers U.S.âChina competition beyond military confrontation — focusing on industrial policy, technology, and governance models. It challenges conventional dichotomies like capitalism vs. socialism or democracy vs. authoritarianism, offering functional lenses instead. Importantly, it encourages policymakers and business leaders to rethink institutional incentives shaping growth and innovation.

I highly recommend it.

title: Tax policy and wealth
text:
Too bad Mitt is powerless (not in office or seeking re-election) and didn't loudly push these ideas in the past, yet he is decent man.  His editorial in the NYT is sensible but will never pass the GOP control!
Buy, Borrow, Die, unrealized gains, stepped-up basis, pass-through losses, or the research from Saez, Zucman, and Yagan showing many billionaires pay very low effective tax rates
Consider some simple math:

The top 10% of Americans owns $113 Trillion dollars. That’s 2/3 of the total wealth of our country. Let’s look at our current political questions relative to this level of wealth. Snap funding is about $100 billion dollars. That’s 1/1000 of that vast wealth. How about ACA subsidies. That’s roughly $100 billion also. Another 1/1000 of that wealth. So, what would be 1/1000 of someone making $100 k per year. That comes out to $100. So, all these things we are fighting about are a drop in the bucket for the top 10%. This top 10% possibly expects 10% rate of return or about $10 Trillion per year. If there was a 2% wealth tax, then their rate of return would drop to 8% or 8 trillion per year. The extra $2 Trillion spent on average people could do wonders for health, food security, and social security. There is so much money at the top, enough for everyone and for every purpose and need.

Mitt's proposal is well articulated, unfortunately the GOP controls all the current levers.

Of course, the WSJ editorial board strongly disagrees:   
https://www.wsj.com/opinion/by-all-means-raise-mitt-romneys-taxes-5e936cf6?st=jrbjqT&reflink=desktopwebshare_permalink

title: Memoirs of Stockholm
text:
Our local Collingswood Library Book Club featured Stockholm Sven by Nathanial Ian Miller as the monthly book.  I read this book and loved it!
It is set between 1910 and 1945 in the archipelago Spitsbergen near the arctic circle (off the Baltic coast from Sweden) featuring the memoir of an awkward man who leaves Stockholm for adventures and meets up with heart-warming characters for a harsh life.  The prose is thoughtful. There are no heroes, just survivors.

title: Europe and American security policy
text:
Two dueling editorials that are useful to understand the recent 2025 National Security Strategy Report, as the administration tries to frame the biggest threats to America: Europe (with no mention of Russia or China).
This is a dramatic framing of what is animating the administration, both at home and abroad! It is a clash of civilizations, and what it means to belong and be at home!  You decide.

One editorial is from the conservative think tank: Claremont Institute:  https://www.nytimes.com/2025/12/11/opinion/national-security-strategy-us-europe.html?smid=url-share

The second is from Tom Friedman, both in the NYT.

title: China's trade surplus
text:
I always find these concepts very confusing, currency strength, trade deficits, who actually benefits, and is this actually controlled. The classic "trilemma" in economics is that you can have only 2 of the 3:   Free capital flows, Independent monetary policy, and Fixed exchange rate.

US chooses:
(1) Free flows + (2) independent policy â floating dollar

China chooses:
(2) independent policy + (3) fixed-ish exchange â capital control

The irony is that the Chinese are exporting like crazy ("factory floor" to the rest of the world"), have a trade surplus, but their Renminbi is weak relative to the dollar, which means the Chinese worker gets paid less and their purchasing power is lower (i.e. poorer so they can't consume). This comes back to human worker expectations, what they are willing to "tolerate" and the governance structure! If the worker expectations rise, how the system handles it. This is not to suggest that ultra-high expectations and consumption mania is better! 

A strong currency means that it can buy a lot of foreign goods; a weak currency buys less. This matters because it changes the balance between exporters, consumers, and domestic jobs. When a currency is strong, imports become cheaper for households and companies, inflation is lower, and travel abroad is more affordable. But a strong currency makes a country’s exports more expensive in world markets, which can hurt manufacturers and farmers. When a currency is weak, the opposite is true: exports become cheaper for the rest of the world (helping factory jobs and employment), while imports become more expensive for domestic consumers.

These dynamics tie into trade deficits and surpluses. Countries with strong export sectors often have trade surpluses, selling more goods abroad than they buy. China is an example: it has built growth around exporting manufactured goods. To support this, China tends to allow the renminbi (RMB) to stay relatively weak. A weaker RMB makes Chinese goods cheaper for foreign buyers, sustaining factory demand and employment. The downside is that Chinese consumers pay more for imported products, and international travel becomes expensive.

The United States follows almost the opposite model. As the global reserve currency, the US dollar is in constant demand around the world—for trade, for energy pricing, and as a safe asset. This helps keep the dollar strong, even though the US runs large trade deficits. A strong dollar benefits American consumers and import-heavy industries because foreign goods, materials, and fuel are cheaper. The trade-off is that US manufacturers and exporters face tougher competition because their products cost more abroad.

Governments can influence currency strength through interest rates and sometimes through direct intervention, but they cannot fully control it—market forces, investment flows, and economic conditions dominate. China actively manages its exchange rate and uses capital controls to preserve policy freedom. The US, by contrast, allows a largely floating dollar, shaped by global demand and Federal Reserve policy. Ultimately, neither strong nor weak currency is inherently “good” or “bad”; each reflects national priorities. China favors export-led growth and employment, so a weaker currency serves its needs. The US prioritizes cheap imports, financial strength, and global leadership, so a stronger dollar aligns with its interests.

title: A Freakonomics conversation on economics
text:
This episode of Freakonomics Radio critically discusses some upcoming regulatory framework for retirement accounts.  There will be a major marketing push to offer these “alternative options” but is probably NOT a great option for most people as per this discussion. 

On August 7, 2025, Trump signed an executive order titled Democratizing Access to Alternative Assets for 401(k) Investors.  ï¿¼
 â¢ The order directs the U.S. Department of Labor (DOL), in coordination with the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) and the Treasury Department, to revisit and update regulatory guidance around what investments are permitted in 401(k) and other defined-contribution plans.  ï¿¼
 â¢ Specifically, the changes would make it easier for 401(k) plans to offer so-called alternative assets — things like private equity, private credit, real estate, infrastructure, commodities, and even digital-asset funds (crypto, etc.) — which historically have been largely reserved for institutional investors or high-net-worth individuals.  ï¿¼
 â¢ The order doesn’t force every 401(k) plan to include these assets. Rather, it gives plan sponsors/fiduciaries more regulatory cover (e.g. safer “safe harbors” from litigation) if, after due diligence, they offer such options.  ï¿¼
 â¢ Alongside, the SEC is being asked to reexamine its definitions of “accredited investor” or “qualified purchaser” — categories that have long restricted who can invest in private funds. Relaxing those definitions would smooth the path for 401(k)-based private-market investments.  ï¿¼

In short: the plan is a major policy push to “democratize” access to previously elite asset classes, potentially opening the door for many ordinary Americans’ retirement funds to be invested in private markets, beyond public stocks and bonds.  The winners will be the banking sector, not the average working bloke! Be wary!
